basis.saw: Figure 1 on page 12: a seven-phase table of planning steps with WHO/ITU tools against each, and the Reference Architecture marked at the right

narrative.text: Figure 1. A planning chart in seven coloured rows, one per phase of planning and implementing digital health: 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment, 02 establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning, 03 defining the future state, 04 planning the enterprise architecture, 05 determining health content requirements, 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use, 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling. Each row lists its steps, then the WHO, ITU and partner tools that support it (among them the WHO-ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, the DIIG, OpenHIE, TOGAF, WHO SMART Guidelines' digital adaptation kits, ICD-11 and HL7 FHIR). A dashed box at the right, 'WHO-ITU Reference Architecture for DPI-H', spans the phases. A footnote expands the abbreviations HIS, ICT, ITU, M&E and SDG.

basis.saw: Figure 2.2 on page 41: the REDDHI infographic

narrative.text: Figure 2.2. An infographic titled 'REDDHI — Resilient Essential Data & Digital Health Infrastructure', subtitled 'a direction of travel, not a fixed destination or a single system'. Panels explain why 'resilient' (survives funding volatility, reduces vendor dependency, long-term sustainability, local capacity) and why 'essential' (minimum capabilities, a foundation for many use cases, investment efficiency, a subset of the national architecture); the full-STAC foundations (Standards such as HL7 FHIR, ICD, SNOMED CT, LOINC and CQL; open-source Technologies; DPI-based Architectures; WHO SMART Guidelines Content); REDDHI's role in the national architecture; five objectives; and the guiding principles as a set of tags.

basis.saw: Figure 3.1 on page 56

narrative.text: Figure 3.1. A worked chain of realisation relationships, top to bottom: a Business Capability ('Identity maintained across services') is realised by an Application Service ('Resolving and matching identity'), which is realised by an Application Function ('Identity matching'), which is realised by an Application Component ('Client Registry'). Each link is a dashed 'realises' arrow, and a note beside each element gives the example.

basis.saw: Figure 3.2 on page 59: the integrated layered view

narrative.text: Figure 3.2. 'DPI-H Reference Architecture — Integrated View': a dense layered poster. From the top: strategic health goals (G1 trusted data foundations to G7 climate and epidemic resilience); cross-cutting governance; stakeholders; capabilities; the point-of-service and functional applications layer; the DPI-H layer of government-stewarded reusable components and the shared data layer of core registries (client, health record, workforce, location, products, terminology and logical information models), REDDHI components starred; the foundational DPI layer (identity, trust services, payments, data exchange, CRVS, geo-location); and the technology layer. An interoperability column at the right lists the information mediator, open standards and integration patterns. At this resolution most of the small text is not legible.

basis.saw: Figure 3.3 on page 61: an Archi view of the TPHR goal

narrative.text: Figure 3.3. An ArchiMate view of the health goal 'Establish Trusted Personal Health Records'. The goal and its four sub-goals (universally accessible verifiable records, consent-based sharing, trust and privacy, interoperability) sit at the top, with four outcomes beneath them. Below, a grey 'TPHR Implementation' grouping holds the capabilities (for example Health Record Management, Identity & Authentication, Consent Management, Trust Verification), the application services that realise them, and the application components (Lifelong Health Record, Client Registry, Consent Management Platform, PKI, SIEM, Terminology Service and others) that realise those.

basis.saw: Figure 3.4 on page 62

narrative.text: Figure 3.4. A layered ArchiMate view for one TPHR sub-goal. 'Establish a secure, universally accessible, verifiable health record for every individual' is realised by the outcome 'Population has verifiable digital health records'; inside 'TPHR Sub-goal #1 Implementation' three capabilities (Health Record Management, Identity & Authentication, Universal Access Enablement) are served by a 'Trusted Personal Health Record (PHR)' product, three application services and three components (Lifelong Health Record, Client Registry, PKI/Trust Infrastructure), which draw on a 'Metadata Components' group of Client, Facility, Health Worker and Product registries and a Terminology Service.

basis.saw: Figure 3.5 on page 63 (Quality and Continuity of Care)

narrative.text: Figure 3.5. A layered ArchiMate view for a Quality and Continuity of Care sub-goal: 'Comprehensive Needs Assessment' and the outcome 'Integrated, Person-Centered Care' at the top; five capabilities (Care Protocol Management, Patient History Integration, Decision Support, Task-Sharing Orchestration, Quality and Performance Monitoring) realised through an 'Integrated Shared Care Plan (SCP)' product; application services for care protocols, clinical decision support, patient-history aggregation and care coordination; components such as a knowledge base engine, EMR, interoperability layer, access control, lifelong health record and client registry; and a grouping of the shared registries and terminology server they use.

basis.saw: Figure 3.4.1 on page 70

narrative.text: Figure 3.4.1. 'Semantic Governance Infrastructure' in three bands. Governance services: LIMR, profile authoring, conformance resources and a governance terminology management service fed by 'Global Content Sources' through content syndication. Runtime services: a runtime terminology service linked to the governance TMS. Content and application layers: implementation guides (IG 1, IG 2, IG 3, …) and applications or use cases (App 1, App 2, App 3, …).

basis.saw: Figure 3.4.2 on page 72; a slide-style figure

narrative.text: Figure 3.4.2. A terminology services maturity model drawn as a rising line through five stages: Nascent (no centrally defined content or governance), Emerging (some content published in non-standard formats), Shared Electronic Reference, Digital Subscription and Data Exchange. A break in the line between Emerging and Shared Electronic Reference marks the steep climb. Notes say many LMICs are at the early stages. Braces beneath group the early stages as selecting and defining standards and the later ones as using terminologies to support data exchange.

basis.saw: Figure 3.4.3 on page 73; a slide-style figure

narrative.text: Figure 3.4.3. 'NHDD Framework: Content Structure': five stacked bars, from reference and administrative code sets (SNOMED, ICD, HL7), through curated concept sources and interface terminologies (CIEL, IMO), country-level subsets, organisation-level dictionaries, down to facility-level dictionaries such as formularies. A downward arrow at the left says international standards are selected and customised for country use and adapted for local implementation; an upward arrow at the right reads 'Submissions / Feedback to Standards' and 'Responsive Local & National Governance'.

basis.saw: Figure 3.6 on page 87

narrative.text: Figure 3.6. Five exchange patterns, each drawn with the same small systems: direct point-to-point connections; a central service bus; gateways protecting each component; distributed access points with a central registry and oversight; and publish-subscribe through an event broker that notifies subscribers.
